questions.problem:
The probability mass function of the independent random variables $X$ and $Y$ are given below.
$x$ $0$ $1$ $2$
$f(x)$ $0.3$ $0.6$ $0.1$

$y$ $0$ $1$ $2$
$f(y)$ $0.3$ $0.4$ $0.3$

Find $\text{Var}[5X-4Y].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y].
$$

Also, the variance of $X$ is determined by the formula 

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

First, let's find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X}$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot f(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 0.6+2\cdot 0.1 \\  & =0.8\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 0.6+4\cdot 0.1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =1-{0.8}^{2} \\  & =0.36.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y}$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}y\cdot f(y) \\  & =0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 0.4+2\cdot 0.3 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}{y}^{2}\cdot f(y) \\  & =0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 0.4+4\cdot 0.3 \\  & =1.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =1.6-{1}^{2} \\  & =0.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[5X-4Y] & ={5}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+(-4)^{2}\text{Var}[Y] \\  & =25(0.36)+16(0.6) \\  & =18.6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider two independent random variables $X$ and $Y$ with expectations $\text{E}[X]=2$, $\text{E}[Y]=4$
and second raw moments $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=5$ and $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]=23.$ Find the variance of  $5X+7Y.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula 

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

First, let's find $\text{Var}[X]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\text{5}-{\text{2}}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\text{2}3-{\text{4}}^{2} \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[5X+7Y] & ={5}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{7}^{2}\text{Var}[Y] \\  & =25(1)+49(7) \\  & =368.\end{aligned}
$$

The probability mass function of the independent random variables $X$ and $Y$ are given below.
$x$ $10$ $15$ $20$ $25$
$f(x)$ $0.25$ $0.35$ $0.15$ $0.25$

$y$ $12$ $18$
$f(y)$ $0.33$ $0.67$

Find $\text{Var}[1.5X+2Y].$ Round your answer to two decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y].
$$

Also, the variance of $X$ is determined by the formula 

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

First, let's find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X}$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot f(x) \\  & =10\cdot 0.25+15\cdot 0.35+20\cdot 0.15+25\cdot 0.25 \\  & =17\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x) \\  & =100\cdot 0.25+225\cdot 0.35+400\cdot 0.15+625\cdot 0.25 \\  & =320.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =320-{17}^{2} \\  & =31.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y}$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}y\cdot f(y) \\  & =12\cdot 0.33+18\cdot 0.67 \\  & =16.02\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}{y}^{2}\cdot f(y) \\  & =144\cdot 0.33+324\cdot 0.67 \\  & =264.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =264.6-{16.02}^{2} \\  & =7.9596.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[1.5X+2Y] & ={1.5}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{2}^{2}\text{Var}[Y] \\  & =2.25(31)+4(7.9596) \\  & ≈101.59.\end{aligned}
$$

$y$ $2$ $4$ $6$
$f(y)$ $\frac{1}{2}$ $\frac{1}{4}$ $\frac{1}{4}$

Find $\text{Var}[3X-2Y].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y].
$$

Also, the variance of $X$ is determined by the formula 

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

First, let's find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X}$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot f(x) \\  & =0(\frac{1}{3})+1(\frac{1}{3})+2(\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{3})+{1}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{3})+{2}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}-{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y}$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}y\cdot f(y) \\  & =2(\frac{1}{2})+4(\frac{1}{4})+6(\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}{y}^{2}\cdot f(y) \\  & ={2}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{2})+{4}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{4})+{6}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =15.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =15-{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X-2Y] & ={3}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+(-2)^{2}\text{Var}[Y] \\  & =9\cdot \frac{2}{3}+4\cdot \frac{11}{4} \\  & =17.\end{aligned}
$$

\textrm{Var}[aX+bY]=a^2\textrm{Var}[X]+b^2\textrm{Var}[Y].
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain 

$$
\textrm{Var}\left[X-2Y\right]=\left(1\right)^2\cdot 10+\left(-2\right)^2\cdot 12 =58.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider two independent random variables $X$ and $Y$ with expectations $\textrm E[X]=5,$ $\textrm E[Y]=4$
and second raw moments $\textrm E[X^2]=30$ and $\textrm E[Y^2]=18.$ Find the variance of  $12X-11Y.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX+bY]=a^2\textrm{Var}[X]+b^2\textrm{Var}[Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula 

$$
\textrm {Var}[X]=\textrm E[X^2]-\textrm E[X]^2.
$$

First, let's find $\textrm{Var}[X]\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =30-{5}^{2} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =18-{4}^{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[12X-11Y] & ={12}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+(-11)^{2}\text{Var}[Y] \\  & =144(5)+121(2) \\  & =962.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
If $X$ and $Y$ are *independent* random variables, then

$$
\textrm{Var}{[X+Y]} = \textrm{Var}[X]+ \textrm{Var}[Y] ,
$$

and

$$
\textrm{Var}{[X-Y]} = \textrm{Var}[X] + \textrm{Var}[Y]  .
$$

**Watch out!** When computing the variance of a *difference* of independent random variables, we *add* the variances!

tutorials.name: The Variance of a Sum of Scaled Random Variables
tutorials.problem:
We have been using the fact that if $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then

$$
\textrm{Var}{[X+Y]} = \textrm{Var}[X]+ \textrm{Var}[Y]  .
$$

Using the property that $\textrm{Var}[aX] = a^2\textrm{Var}[X],$ we can show that if $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then

$$
\textrm{Var}{[aX+bY]} = a^2\textrm{Var}[X]+ b^2\textrm{Var}[Y] ,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

For example, for two independent random variables $X$ and $Y$, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[4X+3Y] & ={4}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{3}^{2}\text{Var}[Y] \\  & =16\text{Var}[X]+9\text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}
$$

Once again, we need to show caution when considering a difference. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[4X-3Y] & =\text{Var}[4X+(-3)Y] \\  & ={4}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+(-3)^{2}\text{Var}[Y] \\  & =16\text{Var}[X]+9\text{Var}[Y].\end{aligned}
$$

More generally, if the random variables $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n,$ are *mutually independent*, then

$$
\textrm{Var}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i\right] = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\textrm{Var}[X_i].
$$
